title: The Factors that Affect Learning: 4 ways in which evidence can get in the way of learning happening
author: Martin Skelton
summary: Skelton sets out four ways evidence about learning can hinder rather than help. First, schools tend to collect only what is easily tested, so knowledge crowds out skills, understanding and attitudes. Second, pressure for quick, digestible data, such as one-word inspection grades, hides complexity; he recounts a respected school downgraded after seven-year-olds were quizzed on facts from before the summer. Third, too much focus on exam-grade feedback turns chemistry into exam preparation, which he likens to weighing a pig rather than feeding it. Fourth, teacher judgements about skills and understanding are unreliable without descriptors and moderation. He closes with a checklist contrasting the helpful and unhelpful sides of assessment.
points: Evidence of knowledge is quickest to gather, so it can crowd out evidence of skills, understanding and attitudes that matter equally.
Simple summary judgements are popular with governments and parents but hide complexity, and a short inspection can rest on thin evidence.
Too much assessment talk shrinks a subject to exam technique, weighing the pig instead of feeding it.
Judgements about skills and understanding become unreliable unless teachers have age-based descriptors and routine moderation.
quotes: As a result, knowledge evidence will tend to take precedence over all other kinds of learning. It’s simply quicker to gather.

There’s nothing wrong with evidence of knowledge acquisition, of course. It is important. But there is something very wrong from a learning perspective when this is the only - or most common - evidence collected, for two reasons.

Almost no school is totally outstanding, totally good, totally requiring improvement or, usually, totally inadequate. These easy, quick judgements hid complex evidence that would have been more helpful in many different ways.

Obviously - because this is what happens even with sticky knowledge if left untouched for a time - its stickiness diminished. Students simply couldn’t remember facts that had been learned months earlier and before the summer break.
The sentence would be more accurate if it read: You can’t enable a pig to grow by only weighing it. Too much weighing gets in the way of all the other activities that make up pig rearing.

There is nothing wrong with exam preparation; there is something wrong with only exam preparation, week after week after week. The potential excitement about chemistry (or any other subject) that I hope my child might experience and perhaps get attracted by is pushed into a siding and ‘chemistry’ simply becomes a vehicle for learning how to pass this particular exam.
If they are, the judgements are just a view. We can’t use them as evidence because we can’t be confident that they mean the same for other teachers and other students.
